extracted.intended_audience: UX/product designers, software developers, IP attorneys and corporate executives in high-technology consumer products
extracted.subtask_short: ux ip strategy for mobile devices
extracted.subtask_description: Recommendations and evaluative criteria for designing, protecting, and litigating user experience (UX) and product design innovations in mobile and connected consumer devices, with emphasis on intellectual property strategy and trial tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect the Total User Experience (TUX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop products and services in this space that focus on the total user experience (TUX): focus innovations on ALL critical customer touch points covering hardware and software interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page defines TUX as the combined look, feel and function across physical product design, screen design, interaction behaviors and graphic screens, and recommends designing to the full set of customer touch points (retail, Genius Bar, website, device-to-device behavior, etc.). It emphasizes that cognitive science treats experience as an integrated whole (the whole > sum of parts), so product strategy and IP should aim to protect that combined experience rather than isolated features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create clusters of IP protection that capture the TUX
rubrics_metrics.description: IP practitioners should make use of all available forms of IP protection including design patents, utility patents, copyright, trademark and in litigation, trade dress, to create an interlocking set of protections that cover the look, feel and function of your products and services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple IP forms together to ‘fence in’ the TUX; Apple's asserted patents combined to approximate the iPhone TUX. The article notes this cluster approach provides broader conceptual protection than any single patent and is an explicit legal strategy recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a robust interactive brand that supports TUX
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider carefully protecting core brand positioning elements and messaging as part of the overall IP protection strategy; in the best user experience design solutions your brand will be delivered by (and be indistinguishable from) your total user experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brand positioning influences jury perception and marketplace recognition; map brand narrative into trial communications. A clear, simple, and consistently delivered brand aids both commercial success and litigation (brand will effectively be 'on trial' with the product).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice tighter integration between legal and development teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Waiting until an innovative new user experience is complete before developing a legal strategy for protection will no longer be productive given the large body of prior art, rapid release schedules and litigious nature of the marketplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate IP counsel early in design cycles to shape filings and evidence, avoid missed prior art or evidentiary errors, and coordinate choices (e.g., what to patent vs. trade dress) so protection aligns with product architecture and release timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on a mobile-first design strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus innovations on mobile-first design and then migrate the interaction model across other screen types to capture user behaviors that start on mobile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites mobile-migration trends (e.g., many tasks starting on smartphones) and recommends designing for mobile as primary, then adapting to tablet/desktop to ensure consistent transfer-of-learning and reduced cognitive load across devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on specific software operating systems or platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Think of TUX design innovations as platform agnostic; do not rely on a single OS or platform as the basis for protecting UX IP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although utility patents or platform-specific claims may be part of strategy, treating TUX as platform-independent improves robustness of protection (users care about what happens at the glass more than underlying OS).

rubrics_metrics.name: To the extent possible secure trade dress rights through litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are going to go for litigation consider doing so based on trade dress as this form of legal protection is likely the most robust option. Be aware of the complexity of such cases before proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade dress can offer broader, potentially indefinite protection tied to consumer recognition and behavior; the article suggests aiming for comprehensive trade dress judgements to protect the overall TUX across touchpoints, while warning about the difficulty and complexity of trade dress litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use design patents to secure visual (non-functional) aspects of UX
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the visual (non-functional) aspects of your solutions absolutely worth protecting and make sure that your IP counsel understands design patent filings and related methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design patents played a major role in Apple’s award; the piece recommends using design patents beyond Apple’s examples to secure screen appearance, iconography, device shape, and other ornamental elements of the UX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control the trial narrative consistent with brand messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure and control a simple, high-level trial narrative (e.g., ‘innovator’ vs ‘copier’) consistent with your market brand positioning to influence jury perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apple successfully extended its marketplace brand narrative into trial communications to simplify jury understanding; defendants should prepare alternative narratives and counter-messaging or risk ceding the high-level frame of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cognitive science and expert testimony (e.g., about shape perception and the ordinary observer test)
rubrics_metrics.description: When design or shape perception issues are central, bring perceptual/cognitive science experts to educate the judge and jury on how ordinary observers perceive shape and similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article criticizes Samsung for not presenting expert testimony on shape perception; expert evidence can materially affect findings under the ordinary observer test and should be integrated into litigation planning where design similarity is contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value infringement at the level of the combined experience; be wary of piecemeal valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the difficulty of assigning meaningful dollar values to individual features when the commercial value derives from a cluster of interacting features forming the TUX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Posner’s critique of economic experts highlights the problem of fragmentary valuations; companies and experts should develop valuation approaches that account for feature interdependence and marketing/behavioral effects rather than summing isolated feature values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct exhaustive prior-art searches and preserve/manage evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Search broadly for prior art (including older references from the 1990s) and manage evidentiary processes carefully to ensure relevant prior art is admitted and preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes the difficulty and cost of finding older prior art and gives an example where Samsung’s prior art was excluded due to counsel error; robust prior-art discovery and evidence handling are essential to avoid surprise invalidity or obviousness issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for positive transfer-of-learning and ease-of-use across touchpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliver a common, highly engaging and easy-to-learn user experience that resides cognitively in the same form across many customer touch-points to enable positive transfer-of-learning from device to device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A consistent UX reduces cognitive workload and friction at point of sale; design decisions should prioritize learnability and predictable behavior across devices (e.g., iPhone→iPad→iPod) as both a business and IP-protection advantage.
